questions.question: Oliver, you called Gwendolen one of the great comic creations in English fiction, which is not how most people come at this novel. Make the case. Read us that arrow passage from chapter nine and tell us why we should be laughing.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the c9:p17 passage and establish the comic frame before the others push back—set up the disagreement early

questions.question: Edmund, you're already shaking your head, I can tell. Because you hear that same passage and you call it 'conquest-speech.' You say there's cruelty in the wit. How does that land differently from what Oliver just gave us?
questions.intent: Force the comic vs moral tragedy fault line into the open—get Edmund to quote the same passage with completely different emotional weight

questions.question: Daniel, you've been listening to two readings of the same passage and you want to pull both of them up short, don't you. Because your argument is that asking whether Gwendolen is charming or morally blind is already the wrong question. What's the right one?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's systemic diagnosis—the marriage market as extraction—and position it against both Oliver's comedy and Edmund's moral tragedy

questions.question: Edmund, there's a passage Daniel flagged—Catherine saying 'He is of a caste to which I look up—a caste above mine.' You think that's Catherine speaking a truth about the soul that Gwendolen can't bear to hear. Daniel thinks it's a woman internalising her own subordination and calling it moral worth. Who's right?
questions.intent: Trigger the sharpest direct disagreement of the segment—Edmund's moral reading vs Daniel's structural critique, with the c22:p31 passage as the flashpoint

questions.question: Oliver, you said the comedy dies the moment Grandcourt stops being Gwendolen's audience. That's a striking way to put it. So what exactly kills it—is there a single moment in these passages where you feel the energy go out?
questions.intent: Draw out Oliver's reading of the c11:p108 period structure as entrapment, close the segment on the pivot from comedy to something darker, and invite the others to locate their own version of that turn

steering_notes: The productive tension in this segment is a three-way disagreement about what kind of novel we're even reading: Oliver says comic, Edmund says moral tragedy, Daniel says anatomy of a system. Don't let any one frame dominate too early—use the first two questions to establish Oliver's comedy and Edmund's counter, then let Daniel reframe both. The Catherine passage (c22:p31) is the ideal pressure point for the Edmund vs Daniel argument because they read it in diametrically opposite ways. Keep pushing for the passages to be read aloud—this segment lives or dies on whether listeners hear the actual prose.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver and Edmund read the c9:p17 arrow passage with opposite tonal registers—Oliver as performance and delight, Edmund as cruelty and conquest-speech. Ask them to account for the other's reading rather than just reassert their own.

Daniel's claim that Gwendolen's wit is her only tradeable asset in the marriage market directly contradicts Oliver's claim that she has genuine narrative energy and verbal power—Oliver would say that's real, Daniel would say it doesn't matter because the system has already priced it.

Edmund's reading of the c22:p31 Catherine passage as moral truth-telling collides head-on with Daniel's reading of it as internalised subordination—this is the most combustible cross-engagement point in the segment, save it for question four.

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that this segment is almost *unplayable* unless you understand it as performance. So let's start with the witch line. C7, paragraph 94: 'it was no wonder a boy should be fascinated by this young witch — who, however, was more mischievous than could be desired.' You called those comedic words masking something dangerous. But Edmund, I know, has a very different read on that word 'however.' Oliver, what's Eliot doing there — is she winking at us, or warning us?
questions.intent: Open the segment on the comedy-vs-moral-seriousness fault line; get Oliver to perform the tonal argument; set up Edmund to contest it

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read that same 'witch' passage as Eliot refusing to let us rest in charm — moral seriousness all the way down. But Oliver's just said it's *theatrical*, that the whole game is surface. Can both of those be true at once? Or is one of you missing something?
questions.intent: Force Edmund and Oliver into direct contact on whether Eliot is doing comedy or conscience — and whether those are even separable

questions.question: Daniel, I want to bring you in on the mother's confession, because all three of you want to quote the same passage — c51, paragraph 71: 'I made believe — I acted that part.' Edmund calls it the most honest thing anyone says in the novel. Oliver calls it almost *comic* in its self-awareness. But you called it something much darker: the colonization of a woman's own will. Make the case. What are they missing?
questions.intent: Let Daniel land his sharpest political reading; provoke Edmund's pushback about will versus circumstance; create a three-way tension on what Leonora's performance actually means

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel's basically just said that your reading — that it's weakness of will, not constraint, that destroys Gwendolen — is the ideological move the novel wants you to make, and you've made it. How do you answer that?
questions.intent: Provoke the sharpest possible Edmund-Daniel clash; get Edmund to defend the moral-individual reading against the structural one without letting either off the hook

questions.question: Let's end on Ezra. C66, paragraph 13: 'I know you — too well — father,' with that slow biting solemnity. Oliver, you called it the moment comedy dies. But I want to ask all three of you — is that line also a kind of performance? Is Ezra doing the same thing everyone else in this segment is doing, just with cold fury instead of charm? Because if he is, what does that say about whether *anyone* in this novel escapes the surface?
questions.intent: Close the segment on an open, genuinely hard question that implicates all three readings — moral, theatrical, political — and lets the experts respond to each other freely

steering_notes: The energy in this segment should feel like three people who've all been handed the same photograph and are arguing about what they see. Don't let it become Edmund vs Daniel on politics — Oliver is the most useful interlocutor because his theatrical reading can sit inside both others or blow them both up. Use him as a wedge. The Leonora passage (c51:p71) is the segment's emotional centre — all three want it, so let them fight over what it *means* rather than just reading it. If the Edmund-Daniel clash on will versus constraint gets too abstract, pull it back to the text: ask them to point to the exact line where Eliot tips her hand. Watch for Oliver quietly agreeing with Daniel on Deronda's sermonising (c65:p20) — that's an unexpected alliance worth surfacing if time allows.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund reads the 'witch' passage (c7:p94) as moral warning; Oliver reads it as comedic surface — they're using the same words to say opposite things and neither has fully registered it yet

Daniel's claim that Deronda's spiritual authority (c65:p20) is 'purchased with Gwendolen's suffering' directly contradicts Edmund's reading of the 'severe angel' as genuine redemptive wisdom — this is the segment's most explosive head-to-head

Oliver half-agrees with Daniel that Deronda is performing salvation but frames it as novelistic irony rather than political critique — worth pushing Oliver on whether that distinction actually holds or is just a more comfortable version of Daniel's argument

All three want to quote Leonora's 'I acted that part' (c51:p71) but for incompatible reasons: Edmund wants authenticity vs performance, Oliver wants tragic-comic self-narration, Daniel wants colonized interiority — force them to name what they think the passage actually *does*

questions.question: Oliver, you've called Gwendolen 'an actress with no stage and no audience.' Can you read us that Grandcourt description — the one about grimace and solicitous wrigglings — and tell us what it feels like to you? Because you're saying his *inertness* is the whole horror. That the thing that should be a weakness is actually what destroys her.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c11:p1 aloud and establish his performance-theory frame as the opening move — sets up the disagreement with both Edmund and Daniel

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push you on something. You're nodding along to that — I can see it — but you'd say Oliver's framing, as elegant as it is, still keeps this inside Gwendolen's head. You want to drag it outside. Lydia Glasher turns up in that field — 'I left my husband and child for him nine years ago' — and you're saying that's not melodrama, that's the evidence. Evidence of what, exactly?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to read the Lydia Glasher passage from c14:p44 and articulate the structural-economic argument, which directly challenges Oliver's psychological-theatrical frame

questions.question: Edmund, I suspect you've been sitting on your hands. Because if I'm hearing you right, you think both of them — Oliver's 'performance trap,' Daniel's 'capitalism trap' — are actually ducking the harder question, which is what's happening inside Gwendolen's soul. You called c35:p126 'the true heart of the matter.' Her will shaken to its depths but still reasserting itself. Is that redemption, or is it — as Oliver would say — just the same old tactics in a worse situation?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to articulate the moral-will argument and directly name his disagreement with Oliver's reading of c35:p126 as 'not redemption, just tactics'

questions.question: Oliver, Edmund just used the word 'soul.' You read c11:p119 — that 'slenderest thread in human history' passage — as savagely comic. Edmund thinks it's Eliot acknowledging something metaphysical and then proceeding past it. Daniel thinks it's a political manifesto. Can you read it to us, because I genuinely think three people can hear three completely different things in the same paragraph, and I want the room to feel that?
questions.intent: Get c11:p119 read aloud to crystallise the three-way disagreement — comic vs. spiritual vs. political — in a single passage

questions.question: Last one, and I'll put it to you Daniel because you'll give me the sharpest answer: is there any version of this novel where Gwendolen's suffering *matters* on its own terms — not as a symptom of a system, not as a moral lesson — just as one woman's experience of being trapped? Or does insisting on the structural reading actually do to Gwendolen what Grandcourt does — refuse to acknowledge her as a subject?
questions.intent: Provoke Daniel with a challenge that uses his own framework against him — risks collapsing the distinction between structural critique and dehumanisation — designed to get all three experts into a genuine three-way argument about what kind of sympathy the novel demands

steering_notes: The three positions map onto genuinely incompatible frameworks — theatrical/psychological (Oliver), moral-spiritual (Edmund), structural-materialist (Daniel) — and the best moments will come when they're forced to account for the *same passage* from different angles. Push for readings aloud wherever possible; the tonal complexity of c11:p119 especially will do the work for you. Watch for Oliver and Edmund's c35:p126 disagreement (tactics vs. redemption) — that's the sharpest bilateral conflict and worth slowing down for. Daniel is most likely to be isolated by the other two, so give him room to reframe rather than just defend.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that c35:p126 is 'the same old tactics' directly contradicts Edmund's reading of it as spiritual crisis — get them to address each other by name on this

Daniel's reading of Grandcourt's inertness as 'the luxury of a man who doesn't have to perform' complements Oliver's performance-theory but undermines its framing as tragedy rather than anatomy — Oliver should be asked to respond

Edmund's insistence that Gwendolen is 'actively complicit in her own blindness' is the point Daniel most wants to contest — his pushback that she's 'economically coerced' with 'no exit' should be surfaced as a direct exchange
All three want to quote c11:p1 — let each read or gloss a phrase from it and see where the same words lead them differently

segment_name: Class, Dominion, and the Marriage Plot

questions.question: Oliver, you've said the satin shoes line is 'cruel, funny, and sympathetic all at once'—and you have to hold all three at the same time or it collapses. But Dan Rosen is going to tell us that the *sympathy* in that line is actually doing something a bit suspect—that feeling sorry for Gwendolen in her satin shoes is Eliot's way of aestheticizing powerlessness rather than questioning why the swamp exists in the first place. So before we even get there: can you read us the passage and make the case for why the tonal balancing act *matters*?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read the satin shoes passage aloud and articulate the performance argument, which sets up Rosen's structural critique as a direct challenge

questions.question: Dan, you just heard Oliver perform that passage—and I think your response is essentially: yes, beautifully done, but the sympathy itself is the problem. The novel lets us *feel* for Gwendolen without ever asking who built the swamp. Is that fair? And does it matter that Eliot seems to *know* she's doing this—that the narratorial voice is in on the joke?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to engage directly with Trevelyan's performance reading and articulate the ideological critique of sympathy in plain terms

questions.question: Edmund, you've got a completely different reading of this novel's centre of gravity—you want to say Mordecai's vision in chapter 61 is where Eliot is *really* speaking, and that the whole marriage plot is the crucible that burns off Gwendolen's egoism. But Dan's going to say that Mordecai's messianic spirituality is actually the most ideologically convenient thing in the book—it lets everyone feel they've transcended class and domination without a single property law changing. Who's right? Is Mordecai the answer, or is he the escape hatch?
questions.intent: Provoke direct confrontation between Leigh's moral-spiritual reading and Rosen's structural critique, using Mordecai as the flashpoint

questions.question: Dan, there's a moment you flagged that I want to push on—the mother saying 'I hated living under the shadow of my father's strictness.' You read that as Eliot at her most radical: a character actually *naming* the institution. But then you say the novel punishes her for that clarity. Oliver thinks it's about the performance of delusion and sincerity; Edmund thinks it's about spiritual slavery. What does the novel actually *do* to the mother, and why does that matter for how we read Gwendolen's version of the same rebellion?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's argument that the novel's structure punishes material critique, and create a three-way disagreement about what the mother's arc means

questions.question: Oliver, last one—and I want you to go back to Miller's riff about Asher's short arm and Naphthali's pig's ears, because you've called it 'grotesque ventriloquism' and almost Dickensian. Edmund says it's Eliot's portrait of moral blindness. Dan says the comedy lets us off the hook from asking why Jews are the *problem* being discussed at all. When you voice that passage—when you actually perform Miller—are you satirizing him, or are you in some sense *doing* what Eliot is doing, which is making the bigotry entertaining? Is there a difference?
questions.intent: Force Trevelyan to confront the ethics of performing Miller, and bring all three arguments—performance, moral imagination, structural critique—into collision on the same passage

steering_notes: The central fault line in this segment is between three genuinely incompatible readings: Trevelyan thinks the novel works through performance and tonal complexity; Leigh thinks it works through moral philosophy and the education of the soul; Rosen thinks it systematically converts structural critique into individual feeling, which is itself ideological. The best radio comes from making sure each of them is responding to the *others'* actual arguments, not just restating their own. Push Leigh and Rosen into direct confrontation on Mordecai—that's the sharpest disagreement. And keep returning Trevelyan to the ethics of performance, because his argument is the most seductive and the most vulnerable to Rosen's challenge. Don't let anyone treat the satin shoes passage as settled—it means something different to all three of them and that tension is the engine of the segment.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's 'cruel, funny, sympathetic simultaneously' reading of the satin shoes passage directly contradicts Rosen's claim that the sympathy aestheticizes powerlessness—get them to argue about whether tonal complexity is a form of critique or a form of evasion

Leigh's reading of Mordecai as the spiritual centre and answer to English egoism is almost exactly what Rosen calls the ideological payoff that lets everyone feel transcendence without material change—this is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be staged explicitly

Rosen says the novel punishes the mother for naming institutions clearly; Leigh says the mother's rebellion shows only that individual psychological liberation without moral grounding leads to 'another form of spiritual slavery'—they agree the mother's arc is meaningful but for completely opposite reasons

Trevelyan's insistence that Miller is ventriloquism and performance sits in tension with Rosen's argument that the comedy of Miller's antisemitism makes it entertaining in a way that forecloses structural questions—ask Trevelyan directly whether performance can also be complicity

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our prep chat that stuck with me — that you can actually *hear* the trauma in Eliot's syntax. There's that moment where Daniel moves the book 'without turning round' and just holds it there for an instant. What's happening in those small physical gestures? What is Eliot doing that a less gifted novelist wouldn't?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform his close reading of the prose rhythm and the hesitation as emotional rupture — ideally get him to read the 'July sunshine and large pink roses' sentence aloud, which will open the door for Edmund and Daniel to respond to the *same* passage from completely different angles

questions.question: Edmund, you'd push back on that, wouldn't you — the idea that this is primarily about psychology or prose technique. You told me before we started that the real subject of that scene is something more enduring than trauma. What did you mean by that?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's take that the wound is about *doubt itself* as a permanent condition of consciousness, not just a childhood scar — and set up his quote from c16:p10 about 'the first arrival of care.' This creates direct tension with Oliver's psychological reading and Daniel's sociological one

questions.question: Daniel, I have to put this to you directly because I think you'd say both Edmund and Oliver are being a bit — let's say, romantic — about this. You told me before we sat down that there's nothing mysterious happening in that garden. So what *is* happening?
questions.intent: Provoke Daniel's materialist reading of illegitimacy as class mechanism and information control — get him to the c16:p12 quote about 'premature reserve' and frame it as the *system working perfectly*. This should produce real friction with Edmund's 'permanent condition of consciousness' argument

questions.question: There's a line I keep coming back to — 'He felt himself in no sense free' in c15:p46. Now Edmund would say that's a self-imposed prison, Oliver might say it's psychological pathology dressed up as duty — Daniel, you've read it against Gwendolen. What does that comparison reveal that we miss when we just read Deronda's story on its own?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to articulate how both Gwendolen and Deronda are products of the same system but trapped differently — he trapped by what he doesn't know, she by what she does. This should force Edmund and Oliver to reckon with the class argument they've been sidestepping

questions.question: I want to end on a question that I suspect might actually cause a proper argument. Edmund, you've said Deronda's later embrace of Jewish identity and Mordecai's vision shouldn't be read as an *answer* to the childhood wound — that would be too neat. But Daniel thinks he's just transferring the self-abnegation he learned in that English garden onto a grander stage. And Oliver thinks it's all reaction, not discovery. Is there *anything* in what happens later in this novel that isn't downstream of that burned moment in the rose garden?
questions.intent: Force a three-way reckoning on whether Deronda ever escapes the wound — Edmund defending genuine moral agency, Daniel insisting it's structural repetition, Oliver calling it psychological compulsion. No clean resolution; let them disagree openly

steering_notes: The energy in this segment will come from the fact that all three experts are working from the *same two or three passages* and reaching completely incompatible conclusions. Let that friction breathe. Don't rush to synthesise. If Edmund and Daniel are heading for a direct confrontation about whether Deronda's tragedy is universal or historically specific, stay out of the way — that's the best radio in the segment. Oliver is the wild card who can disrupt both of them by insisting the answer is in the *sentences themselves*, not the ideas. Use him as a reset button if the Edmund-Daniel argument gets too abstract. Push for at least one moment where someone reads aloud — the 'July sunshine and large pink roses' sentence is the obvious candidate, but the 'premature reserve' line from c16:p12 is arguably more devastating if someone gives it the right weight.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that Deronda's paralysis is 'something he does to himself out of inverted honour' directly contradicts Daniel's reading that the system *manufactures* the paralysis before Daniel has any agency — ask one to respond to the other explicitly

Oliver's insistence that Deronda's later commitments are 'reaction not discovery' and Daniel's reading that he's transferring childhood self-abnegation onto Zionism are actually the same argument from different directions — point this out and see if they're surprised to agree

The word 'premature' in c16:p12 is a pressure point: Edmund reads it as the birth of self-denial, Oliver reads it as trauma calcifying into personality, Daniel reads it as the mechanism of class control. All three should be pushed to justify their reading of that *single word*

Edmund's resistance to reading Jewish identity as the answer to Deronda's wound puts him in an interesting alliance with Daniel, who also refuses the redemptive reading — but for completely opposite reasons. Surface this: they agree on the conclusion, disagree entirely on why

questions.question: Edmund, I want to start with you, because you've been very clear that this novel is fundamentally about souls, not systems. But when Gwendolen has that nightmare vision at c14:p48 — 'I am a woman's life' — that's not really a private moral epiphany, is it? That's a woman seeing the trap close around her. How do you hold onto the 'individual soul' reading when the passage is so obviously about what *every* woman's life looks like?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend the moral imagination reading against the structural critique embedded in the passage itself — and open the door for Rosen to jump in hard

questions.question: Daniel, you've said Eliot is a better sociologist than she knew — that she wanted to write about souls and ended up writing about mechanisms. But doesn't that sell her short? She put those words in the text. If she's showing us the machinery, isn't that intentional? Or are you saying the novel doesn't know what it's doing?
questions.intent: Push Rosen to clarify whether Eliot is complicit in or critical of the ideological work the novel performs — gets at the sharpest version of his argument and invites Leigh to disagree loudly

questions.question: Oliver, you've described the friendship passage at c16:p61 — 'the one spreads strong sheltering wings' — as gorgeous but unsettling. Can you read it to us and say exactly where the unsettling part lives? Because I can imagine Edmund hearing pure moral constancy and Daniel hearing a patronage relation dressed up as love — and I'm wondering which of them is wrong.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read the passage aloud and name the power imbalance explicitly, creating a three-way disagreement about what the same 12 words are actually doing

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to Mordecai's deathbed at c70:p14 — 'Death is coming to me as the divine kiss which is both parting and reunion.' You've said this is Eliot aestheticizing poverty, converting material abandonment into transcendence. But Edmund thinks it's genuinely moving and Oliver thinks it's theatrically excessive on purpose. Is there any version of this scene that isn't a problem for your reading? Can a dying poor man not be allowed ecstasy?
questions.intent: Put the hardest version of the counterargument to Rosen and invite him to either concede some ground or sharpen his critique — creates maximum friction with Leigh

questions.question: Oliver, your strongest take is that this whole novel is really about the addictive architecture of intimate obligation — being needed, needing to be needed. If that's right, what does that do to Gwendolen? Because she's not really in a reciprocal obligation with anyone — she's just trapped. Is she outside the system you're describing, or is she the dark heart of it?
questions.intent: Push Trevelyan's thesis to its limit on Gwendolen, where it's least comfortable, and see if Rosen and Leigh want to fight over whose version of Gwendolen is right

steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way disagreement with real stakes — don't let it collapse into Rosen vs Leigh with Trevelyan playing referee. Trevelyan's 'addictive obligation' thesis is the most original and should be pushed hardest; it's the one that can genuinely surprise both Rosen and Leigh. Keep pulling back to specific passages and ask people to read aloud — the rhythm of these sentences is itself an argument. If the conversation gets too abstract, drop in: 'but what does the prose actually sound like when it's doing that?' Expect Leigh to get heated when Rosen talks about Mordecai's poverty; that's a good moment, let it breathe. Watch for Trevelyan and Rosen finding unexpected common ground on the Daniel-Hans dynamic — that's the most interesting cross-engagement in this segment.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh reads c14:p48 as individual moral failure; Rosen reads it as structural visibility — ask them both what Gwendolen *could* have done differently and watch the disagreement become concrete

Rosen and Trevelyan both see the c16:p61 friendship passage as encoding a power imbalance, but for completely different reasons — Rosen sees class patronage, Trevelyan sees the pleasure of being needed. They might be describing the same thing from different angles; surface that explicitly

Leigh insists Mordecai's language at c70:p14 is spiritually authentic; Trevelyan thinks it's deliberately operatic; Rosen thinks it aestheticizes poverty. All three are responding to the same 20 words — get them in the room together with the text in front of them

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started that the real awakening in this segment is the *reader's* awakening, not Gwendolen's or Daniel's. That's a provocative claim. Can you make the case — and maybe read us the 'sap into leafage' sentence to show what you mean?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform his strongest stylistic-formalist take and read c11:p118 aloud, setting up the disagreement about whether Eliot is a moralist or a stylist

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read that line — 'the desire to conquer is itself a sort of subjection' — slowly, almost like a piece of scripture. Daniel Rosen is sitting right here and I suspect he thinks that reading is exactly the problem. Persuade him.
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's moral-tragedy reading and directly bait the cross-engagement with Daniel Rosen over whether Eliot's moralizing illuminates or obscures coercion

questions.question: Daniel, you said Gwendolen has *every* design — that she's reading the marriage market with perfect clarity, and the narrator calling it instinct is how we avoid seeing her as a rational actor. But then why does Eliot give us that extraordinary phrase 'poor child'? Is that Eliot's failure of nerve, or is something else going on?
questions.intent: Push Daniel to account for the narrator's apparent sympathy rather than just the structural critique, potentially exposing tension in his own reading

questions.question: Edmund, the Daniel passage — the one about wishing his father's wrongs might never be spoken of to him, the terror of being *known*. You called it the privacy of shame. Daniel Rosen calls it internalized surveillance — the household teaching the boy to crush himself. Those feel like completely different novels to me. Is one of you wrong?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between the spiritual-anguish reading and the class-power reading of Daniel's illegitimacy spiral, ideally getting both experts to speak to each other rather than at the host

questions.question: Last question for all three of you, but Oliver I'll start with you. If this segment is called 'Awakening and Inheritance' — what actually gets inherited? Gwendolen inherits her own self-deception, Daniel inherits his shame. Does anyone in this novel wake up, or is Eliot too honest to allow that?
questions.intent: Open up a closing round where all three can stake a final position — expected disagreement on whether the novel is ultimately redemptive, tragic, or structurally indifferent to individual awakening

steering_notes: The productive fault line in this segment runs between Edmund's moral-tragedy reading and Daniel Rosen's structural-power reading, with Oliver cutting across both by insisting the real action is in the prose itself rather than in what it depicts. Let Edmund and Daniel argue directly — they want to. Your job is to keep Oliver from retreating into pure formalism and to keep Daniel from making it purely about economics; both need to be pushed to account for what the other is seeing. If the conversation stalls, go back to the text: make someone read a passage aloud. The 'sap into leafage' sentence and the 'poor child' phrase are both hot enough to restart any thread.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that the awakening is the reader's directly contradicts Edmund's investment in Gwendolen's and Daniel's moral growth as the novel's real subject — Edmund will want to push back

Daniel Rosen's reading of 'the desire to conquer is itself a sort of subjection' as obscuring economic coercion directly challenges Edmund's claim that this line is Eliot's deepest moral insight — this is the sharpest disagreement in the panel

Oliver's 'performance anxiety' reading of Daniel's spiral and Daniel Rosen's 'internalized surveillance' reading are unexpectedly compatible in one way — both deny the passage pure psychological interiority — but Oliver will resist Rosen's political framing, which creates a second-order disagreement worth surfacing

Edmund's insistence that Gwendolen is 'her own jailer first' and Daniel Rosen's counter that every choice available to her is a choice between forms of economic dependence is a genuine impasse that won't resolve, which makes it ideal for the closing round
